**Lunch on the Floor of an Ancient Sea**

There is a moment, somewhere on almost any long drive, when you pass a highway roadcut and the world opens like a book you didn't know you were carrying. The engineers blasted through a hillside to lay the road flat, and now the hillside stands exposed on either side of you, sliced clean, its private innards turned public. Layers run along the rock in stripes: gray, cream, rust, gray again. And here is the strange part, the part that never stops hitting me no matter how many times I've seen it: those layers were once horizontal. Something enormous happened to them. They got tipped, folded, shoved upward by forces operating on schedules so slow that the whole cataclysm looks, from the outside, like stillness. The rock looks like it's been sitting quietly forever. It hasn't. It's a wave that froze mid-crash four hundred million years ago, back when this exact spot was the floor of a shallow sea, patrolled by things with exoskeletons, lit by a younger sun.

If you pulled over and put your hand on that rock, you would be touching the bottom of an ocean. It's right there. It travels at seventy miles an hour whenever a truck lane needs a shortcut.

This is the doorway into what geologists call deep time, a term John McPhee coined in 1981 and immediately regretted nothing, because we needed it. Ordinary language fails here. "Old" describes cheese and grudges. Deep time is a different substance altogether, and our intuitions about it are like a goldfish's intuitions about altitude. Consider the people who first measured it. In 1788, James Hutton sailed along the Scottish coast to a promontory called Siccar Point, where he had heard tell of something impossible: slanted rock lying beneath flat rock, tilted strata buried under horizontal layers like sleeping bodies stacked under standing ones. When he landed and climbed down to look, his companion John Playfair recorded what happened to them: "The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time." Giddy. Two grown men, standing on a beach, dizzy. Hutton drew the correct conclusion, which was that the earth was immeasurably older than anyone believed, that the rock record contained no archival notes, no chapter headings, nothing but patient accumulation. His famous sentence still reads like a dare: the planet shows "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end."

He was wrong about the beginning, technically; there is one, around 4.54 billion years back. But you can forgive him. He couldn't see it, and neither can you.

I think about Hutton's vertigo a lot, partly because I suspect most of us build our whole emotional lives on the assumption that nothing like it exists. Our native sense of time is shallow and warm. A childhood decades gone feels like yesterday, and yesterday has terrible posture, slouching into last week, which blurs into "recently," which quietly annexes entire years. We calibrate our sorrows and triumphs against this little interior pond and call the calibration reality. Then someone hands you a fossil the age of ten thousand civilizations laid end to end, and you understand, briefly, that your pond sits beside an ocean it cannot see across.

Sometimes the ocean sends ambassadors, and occasionally they arrive alive. In the white limestone peaks of eastern Nevada grow bristlecone pines, the gnarled, half-dead-looking veterans of the tree world. They survive by refusing to live much: they grow painfully slowly in brutal soil at ten thousand feet, their resin so saturated with defensive chemicals that fungi giving up mid-invasion become part of the wood. Their dead sections can outlast their living ones, and the tree doesn't care; it keeps a thin strip of cambium running sap up one side like a woman carrying water along the edge of a ruin. One of these trees, growing near Wheeler Peak, was known to researchers in the 1950s and early sixties as possibly the oldest living thing ever found.

In 1964, a graduate student named Donald Currey went out to study it. The exact sequence of events has blurred into legend, but the essentials are agreed upon: cores were being taken to count the tree's growth rings, some core or corer got stuck or broke, and the Forest Service issued permission to fell the tree outright. So a man who presumably loved trees took a chainsaw to the oldest living individual organism on record, a tree nearly five thousand years old, older than the alphabet, older than the domestication of the horse, and cut it down to count its rings. By the time the count was finished, the answer had changed from a discovery to a casualty. He named it Prometheus.

I don't tell this story to condemn him. Tellers of the tale love to moralize, but the thing I take from it is sadder and stranger than blame. It's the closest thing to a fable science offers about the collisions between shallow time and deep time: we, creatures of deadlines and semesters, meet a being that germinated before the pyramids were a twinkle, and our hands do what hands do, which is reach, grasp, cut. Currey spent his life after this working on glacial geology, and by several accounts carried the episode heavily. As well he might. There's something almost unbearably polite about the whole tragedy. The tree stood through five thousand years of lightning and drought and did not die by weather, beetle, or axe. It died of curiosity, cheerfully licensed, during the administration of Lyndon Johnson.

Meanwhile the actual champions of longevity refuse to make the news properly, because they aren't individuals. In Utah there is an aspen colony called Pando, seventy-some acres of genetically identical trunks connected by one root system, plausibly tens of thousands of years old, maybe among the oldest living things on earth, present in some form when Neanderthals still walked Europe. In Tasmania grows a shrub called King's lomatia, all remaining members of its species clones of one another, the lineage persisting perhaps forty thousand years without sex, because its fruit is sterile and it reproduces only by dropping root suckers. These organisms attend their own permanence the way I attend meetings: barely, and through proxies. Nobody knows what the oldest living thing on earth thinks about anything, including longevity. Endurance seems not to interest plants. They are up to something else entirely, something continuous and mute, and our categories of "individual," "lifetime," "achievement" slide off them like water off wax.

Here's the arithmetic exercise that recalibrates me faster than any other. Compress the whole history of Earth into one calendar year, January 1 through December 31. The planet forms on January 1. Life, those faint chemical scuffles in the oceans, gets going surprisingly early, by late March. Almost everything else waits. Complex animals don't show up until mid-November. Dinosaurs rule from roughly December 10th or so, in glorious complacency, until the evening of December 26th, when an asteroid arrives unannounced, the ultimate in poor festive timing. Homo sapiens appears at about eleven fifty-two on New Year's Eve, thirty-eight minutes before midnight. Recorded history, all of it, every king and ledger and breakup song from Uruk onward, occupies the final half-minute. The United States is less than two seconds old. Your whole life is a rounding error inside a rounding error. And yet here you are, somehow, reading this, fully awake in the smallestmost sliver of the whole calendar, which is the only sliver you get.

For a long time, even scientists fought about how big this pond actually was. Charles Darwin needed the earth to be very old for his theory of gradual modification to work, and in the late nineteenth century the physicist Lord Kelvin calculated, quite brilliantly from first principles of heat flow, that the planet had cooled from molten origins over a span of merely twenty to forty million years. That budget crushed Darwin, who complained privately that physics had apparently declared his entire mechanism impossible. Both men were magnificent and both were wrong, because neither knew about radioactivity. The earth wasn't simply cooling like a dropped stone; it was being gently kept warm from within, like soup over a pilot light, by decaying uranium and thorium in the rocks. Ernest Rutherford figured this out, and by the nineteen-tens the age of the earth had exploded upward by two orders of magnitude. There's a pleasing irony in it: the true scale of deep time was finally revealed by tuning in to the ticking of a clock built into matter itself, atoms falling apart at fixed rates like sand in an hourglass, each element keeping its own obedient schedule across eons.

But this is where the ocean starts pressing in on us in a practical way, and this is the part of the story I find most haunting. Somewhere in the desert near Carlsbad, New Mexico, the United States buries transuranic nuclear waste in excavated salt beds half a mile down. Salt, it turns out, flows like glacier-stiff taffy over geologic timescales; given enough millennia, the mountain closes around the waste rooms like a fist and holds them. The plan is to keep the stuff isolated for ten thousand years, which sounds long and is, by our standards; Ten thousand years ago, no city existed anywhere on earth. No agriculture. Writing hadn't been invented. Whoever marks that site must speak to people separated from us by a gap wider than the gap between us and the builders of Stonehenge, times three.

In the early nineties, teams of linguists, anthropologists, semioticians, and architects gathered to solve this problem, and their deliberations were collected in a document that deserves to be far more famous than it is. How do you write a warning sign that works across the rise and fall of every language, every nation, every symbol system? What if the future digs because of the marker rather than despite it, the way pharaohs' curses became advertisements? One proposal: breed cats whose eyes change color in the presence of radiation, then seed folk songs and legends worldwide so that wherever people go, cat lore travels with them, and when the lore-cats' eyes go strange, everyone knows to leave. Another: create an "atomic priesthood," a ritual order tasked with preserving the knowledge through ceremony and taboo, on the theory that religions outlast governments. The architects produced drawings of landscapes engineered to inspire dread, vast grids of jagged black thorns, fields of illegal-seeming geometry, monumental forms that suggest nothing so much as a huge machine hatred. The verbal texts drafted for the site read like scripture composed by a security system:

> *This place is not a place of honor. No highly esteemed deed is commemorated here. Nothing valued is here.*
> *What is here was dangerous and repulsive to us. This message is a warning about danger.*

*It is still here.* I don't know a better modern expression of what deep time feels like when it turns and looks back at you. We are a culture that can send a message forty feet and ten thousand years, and the message is essentially: we're sorry, we made something we couldn't undo, please forget our enthusiasm and let the desert sit undisturbed.

So there are two ways to hold all this, and I've done time with both. The first is Pascal's way: terror. "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." You stand at Siccar Point, or under a bristlecone, or over the calendar math, and feel yourself erased in advance, your loves and grievances rendered statistically invisible, your species a sneeze in a cathedral, and the mind reels with something adjacent to nausea. That feeling is honest, and I won't pretend it goes away entirely, and maybe shouldn't.

But the second way is available too, and I've come to trust it more. If nothing I do echoes for a billion years, then also nothing I do is obligated to. The anxieties that come from mattering enormously are relieved along with the pleasures. Your embarrassing moment from ninth grade has survived zero billionths of geological time and will survive zero more; the limestone was busy that day and remains busy. Deep time is the great stain remover for the vanity-sized guilts, not because those guilts weren't real but because they were never load-bearing. And there's a subtler gift: knowing the sea floor lies under the interstate makes the interstate miraculous rather than mundane. Everything ordinary sits on top of something unbelievable. Every driveway is a cliff face into the past. You don't need to visit Arizona or Nevada to touch the immemorial; you need to notice the gravel.

Here's the one caution I've earned, I hope. Smallness is not permission to care less. Scale has no moral direction; it is just a ruler lying next to things. The immensity of time does not put your kindness or your cruelty under its protection; morality lives entirely inside the here and now, which is a bug for tyrants and the whole genius of it for the rest of us. If anything, deep time sharpens the case for stewardship: you happen to be awake during the instant, the single lit frame in a hundred-million-year reel, when the biosphere's fate depends on choices being made by one talkative primate. To shrug off responsibility on grounds of cosmic smallness is like refusing to return a library book on the grounds that libraries, eventually, all burn. The due date is due date enough. Meaning doesn't scale. A three-second kindness can outweigh a thousand-year dynasty, and the geology department has no jurisdiction in the matter whatsoever.

Which brings me back to the roadcut, and the ending I keep circling. Picture the person driving home tonight past that slice of Devonian seabed. They're tired, the radio's on, they're singing along badly to something. They have no idea they are riding weightless across an ancient ocean bottom at law-abiding speeds; why would they? And I used to think this obliviousness was the sad part. Now I think it's the merciful part, maybe even the point. The overwhelm is available, standing by, whenever we want it; you can always pull over and get dizzy like Playfair. But most of the time we are permitted to be small and local and warm, to worry about dinner, to sing inside the brief flicker we've been allotted inside the brief flicker of our species. The limestone doesn't know about us, and it will lean into its ten millionth indifferent noon whether the song continues or not. Which means the song, for the length of it, is the only loud thing in the universe. Two or three minutes of somebody's Tuesday, ringing out over four hundred million years of patience.

Whoever you are, thank you for spending half a minute of the cosmic calendar on this page. From where I sat while writing it, it looked longer. Most things, at our scale, do.

1. A personal essay on some topic (memory, time, cities, language)
2. Fiction — a short story
3. A meditation on something specific and strange
4. A blend — essayistic fiction or narrative nonfiction style

I want to write something that feels alive and specific. Generic topics ("the nature of time," "why we love") tend toward abstraction and platitude. The best freewriting usually lands on concrete particulars and follows them somewhere surprising.
